linear-algebra.intuition: A quantum state is an arrow in a vast dark room. Everything that can happen to it is one of three physical acts: gates rotate the arrow, noise jostles it, and measurement slams it flat onto an axis. Learn to handle arrows and you can handle all three.

misconceptions.myth: Quantum computing math needs calculus and differential equations.
misconceptions.truth: The daily toolkit is linear algebra: vectors, matrices, inner products. If you can multiply a 2×2 matrix by a column vector, you can follow most of this field.

complex-numbers-dirac-notation.intuition: Two pendulums swinging in step reinforce; out of step, they cancel. The timing difference — the phase — is physically real, and Dirac notation is the ledger that tracks every pendulum's length and timing without drawing a single picture.

misconceptions.myth: The imaginary parts of amplitudes are a mathematical trick with no physical meaning.
misconceptions.truth: Relative phase between amplitudes is physically real — it decides how computational paths interfere. Only the global phase of the whole state is unobservable.

quantum-mechanics-basics.intuition: Measuring a qubit is popping a soap bubble to inspect its colors: you get one glint of an answer, and the shimmering thing you were asking about is gone. That single fact shapes everything — including why error correction must never look at its data directly.

misconceptions.myth: Measurement gently reads out what the state was.
misconceptions.truth: Measurement projects: it forces one outcome and deletes the amplitudes you did not see. This is exactly why error correction never reads its data qubits directly.

qubits-pauli-operators.intuition: There are only three ways to knock a compass needle: flip it end-for-end (X), shift the timing of its swing (Z), or both at once (Y). Every possible qubit error — however messy and continuous — is a mixture of those three knocks. Fix three things and you have fixed everything.

misconceptions.myth: Noise is continuous, so there are infinitely many different errors to correct.
misconceptions.truth: Measuring the stabilizers digitizes noise: any continuous error collapses onto I, X, Y, or Z. Error correction only ever fixes a four-letter alphabet.

quantum-gates-circuits.intuition: A circuit diagram is sheet music: each wire a string, each gate a note, time flowing left to right. A quantum computer is the orchestra sight-reading it — and syndrome extraction is a four-bar riff the machine must play in perfect time, forever.

misconceptions.myth: Information in a CNOT flows one way, from control to target.
misconceptions.truth: X errors copy control→target, but Z errors copy target→control. Errors flow both directions through a CNOT — which is why gate ordering is a safety decision.

classical-error-correction.intuition: Shouting across a windy field, you say everything three times: the wind can steal one copy and the vote still carries your word. All of error correction is that one trick — redundancy plus a vote — refined into better and better geometry.

misconceptions.myth: Quantum codes made classical coding theory obsolete.
misconceptions.truth: CSS codes literally are two classical codes working together — one for bit flips, one for phase flips. The classical theory is load-bearing inside the quantum one.

stabilizer-formalism.intuition: A drumhead held taut by rules: strike it anywhere and you don't see the dent — you hear exactly which tensions ring wrong. A stabilizer code defines its states by the checks that stay silent, so an error announces itself by the rules it breaks.

misconceptions.myth: Since S|ψ⟩ = |ψ⟩, measuring a stabilizer does nothing at all.
misconceptions.truth: It does nothing to code states. On an errored state it does something crucial: it returns −1, converting a quantum error into classical information without touching the encoded data.

quantum-codes-basics.intuition: [[n, k, d]] is a rope's spec sheet: n strands twisted together to carry k loads, and the rope only lets go after d strands fray. Distance is not decoration — it is the physical count of how much fraying the design survives.

misconceptions.myth: A distance-d code corrects d errors.
misconceptions.truth: It corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors and merely detects up to d−1. Distance 3 fixes one error, not three.

fault-tolerance-thresholds.intuition: Fighting a fire with crews who sometimes drop matches: below the threshold, each ring of firebreak you clear buys more safety than the crew's own sparks cost, and protection compounds. Above it, your firefighters start more fires than they put out — and bigger crews make it worse.

misconceptions.myth: The threshold is a property of the code alone.
misconceptions.truth: It is a property of code + circuits + decoder + noise model together. That is why 'the' surface-code threshold ranges from ~15% in the Lab's toy model down to ~1% with realistic noisy circuits.

topological-order-anyons.intuition: Store the secret in the shape of the whole, not in any piece — like the number of holes in a pretzel. No single bite changes it; only eating a path clear across the pretzel can. Local noise takes bites; topology counts holes.

misconceptions.myth: Anyons are exotic particles that must be discovered in nature.
misconceptions.truth: In these codes they are not fundamental particles at all — they are patterns of stabilizer violations, the endpoints of error strings. The lattice manufactures its own anyons.

toric-code.intuition: Stretch rubber bands around a donut: one can circle the hole, another the body, and no amount of local sliding turns one into the other or into nothing. The toric code stores its two qubits in exactly those two un-slidable windings.

misconceptions.myth: The toric code is what quantum hardware actually builds.
misconceptions.truth: Nobody fabricates donuts. The toric code is the theorist's cleanest classroom; hardware builds its planar child, the surface code, where boundaries replace the wrap-around topology.

surface-code.intuition: A quilt whose every square constantly asks its four corners 'do you agree?'. No square ever sees a stitch directly — yet from nothing but yes/no answers, the quilt locates every tear. That checkerboard of tiny referees is the most practical quantum memory ever designed.

misconceptions.myth: The surface code won because it protects best per qubit.
misconceptions.truth: Several codes beat it on overhead. It won on engineering: nearest-neighbor gates on a 2D chip and the highest practical threshold — it forgives imperfect hardware.

syndrome-extraction-circuits.intuition: The stabilizer is measured like passing a collection plate down a pew: the ancilla visits its four neighbors, each adds its parity, and only the plate is inspected at the end. The danger is the passing itself — drop the plate mid-row and the damage spreads to whoever touched it next.

misconceptions.myth: Any CNOT ordering that computes the right parity is as good as any other.
misconceptions.truth: Orderings differ in how mid-circuit faults spread. A bad schedule turns one ancilla fault into a hook error that halves the effective distance — ordering is fault tolerance, not style.

decoding-mwpm.intuition: Fresh snow, no cat in sight — only paw prints that start and stop. Decoding is reconstructing where the cat walked from the endpoints alone, and the matching decoder always bets on the laziest cat: the shortest total path consistent with every print.

misconceptions.myth: If the syndrome is cleared, the state was recovered.
misconceptions.truth: The syndrome always clears — that is guaranteed. Success is whether error + correction form a harmless loop or a lattice-crossing logical operator. Decoders fail silently, never loudly.

defects-braiding.intuition: Maypole ribbons: by the end of the dance, all that matters is which ribbon crossed over which — every stumble and wobble along the way is forgotten. Braiding computes with holes in the lattice the same way: only the crossing pattern of their paths survives.

misconceptions.myth: Braiding was abandoned because it turned out to be wrong.
misconceptions.truth: It works — it is just expensive in space and time. Lattice surgery achieves the same gates more cheaply. Braiding remains the clearest picture of why topological gates are protected.

lattice-surgery.intuition: Logical qubits live on separate tiles of fabric. Computing is running a zipper between two tiles — the closing zipper asks exactly one joint question of the pair — then unzipping them apart again. A whole algorithm becomes a floor plan of zips and cuts unfolding in time.

misconceptions.myth: Merging two patches destroys and rebuilds the logical qubits.
misconceptions.truth: A merge is a measurement of one joint operator (like Z⊗Z) and nothing else; the split preserves the rest. It is computation by careful asking, not by touching.

cluster-states-mbqc.intuition: Weave the entire tapestry first — every thread crossing every thread. Then compute by pulling threads out one row at a time, where each pull tightens the pattern that remains and decides which thread to pull next. All the entanglement up front; all the choices during the unraveling.

misconceptions.myth: MBQC is a rival architecture that the surface code defeated.
misconceptions.truth: Run a surface code through time and you get exactly a 3D cluster state — the same physics in two languages. The best known thresholds were first found from the cluster-state side.

magic-states-distillation.intuition: Clifford gates are a piano with one key missing — and that key (T) is what makes the instrument worth playing. Magic states are pre-recorded T-notes, each playable exactly once; distillation is remastering fifteen hissy recordings into one clean take.

misconceptions.myth: Magic states are a niche optimization detail.
misconceptions.truth: Non-Clifford resources historically dominated the entire cost of a fault-tolerant computer — in older architectures, most physical qubits existed solely to produce magic states.

flag-fault-tolerance.intuition: A bell hung on the tool cabinet: it cannot stop a thief, but it always rings when the cabinet opens — so you know exactly which tools to distrust afterward. One cheap witness converts an invisible dangerous fault into a labeled, correctable one.

misconceptions.myth: More ancillas always means more fault tolerance.
misconceptions.truth: Older schemes used large verified ancilla blocks; flags achieve the same guarantee with one or two extra qubits. The insight is detecting dangerous faults, not preventing them.

zx-calculus-basics.intuition: Circuits redrawn as plumbing: green and red spiders joined by pipes, plus a small rulebook for sliding joints along pipes and fusing them. Two networks that the rules connect pass exactly the same water — so you can simplify a computation by re-plumbing the picture.

misconceptions.myth: Diagram-pushing is informal hand-waving compared to matrix algebra.
misconceptions.truth: The ZX rewrite rules are complete: every equality of linear maps provable with matrices is provable with diagrams. It is fully rigorous — and compilers exploit it.

advanced-decoding.intuition: Two detectives and one chess clock: MWPM is the meticulous one who is almost always right; union-find is the quick one who is right nearly as often and never lets the clock run out. In a room where the crimes never stop arriving, the clock picks the detective.

misconceptions.myth: Decoder choice just trades away a little accuracy.
misconceptions.truth: It trades accuracy against latency — and latency is correctness at the system level. A perfect decoder that falls behind loses to backlog; the best decoder is the best one that keeps up.

real-time-decoding-control.intuition: A conveyor belt delivers one syndrome every microsecond, forever, like the chocolate factory scene — except every truffle you fail to wrap makes the belt speed up. Fall behind by any steady amount and the backlog compounds until the quantum state rots faster than you can save it.

misconceptions.myth: Decoding can be batched and run after the computation finishes.
misconceptions.truth: For a memory experiment, maybe. For computation, no: non-Clifford gates need decoding results as feed-forward during the run. Real-time is a requirement, not an optimization.

magic-state-cultivation.intuition: Instead of building a refinery to purify truckloads of crude magic, grow one flawless crystal in a small clean chamber — then build the fortress walls outward around it. Same jewel, a fraction of the factory.

misconceptions.myth: Cultivation is a modest percentage improvement over distillation.
misconceptions.truth: It attacked the single largest line item in the machine's budget. Whole-computer resource estimates changed, which is why one technique reshaped hardware roadmaps.

tqec-compilers-automation.intuition: From gate list to factory floor plan: the compiler turns an algorithm into shaped blocks of space-time — patches, pipes, and magic-state factories — then packs them like a master Tetris player, because every empty row of the building costs real qubits and real microseconds.

misconceptions.myth: Compilation is a solved afterthought, like emitting machine code.
misconceptions.truth: Layout and scheduling change total qubit-hours by large factors. The compiler is a first-class research frontier, not plumbing.

clifford-simulation-hybrid.intuition: Photocopying is free; painting is expensive. Clifford operations photocopy — a classical machine reproduces them perfectly at any scale. Only the few non-Clifford brushstrokes need a painter, so hybrid simulators photocopy the book and hand-paint the three illustrations.

misconceptions.myth: Circuits big enough to matter cannot be classically verified.
misconceptions.truth: QEC circuits are almost entirely Clifford, so stabilizer and hybrid methods verify them exactly over billions of shots — that is how designs are validated before hardware exists.

below-threshold-experiments.intuition: The first time the dam actually held: for decades, adding more concrete (qubits) made real dams leak more, not less. In 2024 a machine finally crossed the line where each added ring makes the leak measurably smaller — and the water level has been dropping since.

misconceptions.myth: Crossing the threshold means fault-tolerant quantum computing is finished.
misconceptions.truth: It means scaling now helps instead of hurts. Λ ≈ 2 must grow much larger, and one protected memory must become thousands of computing qubits — the race started; it did not end.
